source_text: Vae, ait, per quem traditur filius hominis. ergo iam \'uae* constat imprecationis et comminationis inclamationem intellegendam et irato et offenso deputandam, nisi si ludas impune erat tantum sceleris relaturus. at si impune, uacat \'uae\'; si non impune, utique ab eo puniendus, in quem scelus traditionis admisit. porro si sciens passus est hominem, quem ipse comitatui suo adsciuerat, in tantum scelus ruere, noli iam de creatore circa Adam retractare quae in tuum quoque deum retorquentur: aut ignorasse illum, qui non ex prouidentia obstitit peccaturo, aut obsistere non potuisse, si (non) ignorabat, aut noluisse, si et sciebat et poterat, atque ita malitiosum iudicandum, qui passus sit hominem suum ex delicto perire. suadeo igitur agnoscas potius et in isto creatorem quam parem illi deum optimum aduersus sententiam tuam facias. nam et Petrum praesumptorie aliquid elocutum negationi potius destinando zeloten deum tibi ostendit. debuit etiam osculo tradi, propheticus scilicet Christus, ut eius scilicet filius, qui labiis a populo diligebatur. Perductus in consessum, an ipse esset Christus, interrogatur. de quo Christo Iudaei quaesissent nisi de suo? cur ergo non uel tunc alium eis prodidit? \'ut pati posset\', inquis, id est, ut ille optimus ignorantes adhuc in scelus mergeret. atquin et si dixisset, passurus esset. si dixero enim, inquit, uobis, non credetis. porro non credituri perseuerassent in necem eius. et cur non magis passurus esset, si alterius dei ac per hoc aduersarium creatoris (se) manifestasset? ergo non, ut pateretur, alium se tunc quoque supersedit ostendere, sed quoniam ex ore eius confessionem extorquere cupiebant, nec confesso tamen credituri, qui eum ex operibus scripturas adimplentibus agnouisse debuerant. ita eius fuit occultasse se, cui ultro debebatur agnitio. et tamen adhuc eis manum porrigens: abhinc, inquit, erit filius hominis sedens ad dexteram uirtutis dei. suggerebat enim se esse (de) Danihelis prophetia (filium hominis* et de psalmo Dauid (sedentem ad dexteram dei\'. itaque ex isto dicto et scripturae comparatione inluminati, quem se uellet intellegi: ergo, inquiunt, tu dei filius es? cuius dei, nisi quem solum nouerant? cuius dei, nisi quem in psalmo meminerant dixisse filio suo: sede ad dexteram meam? <sed respondit: uos dicitis, quasi: non ego\\ atquin confirmauit id se esse, quod illi dixerant, dum rursus interrogant. unde autem probabis interrogatiuo et non (et) ipsos confirmatiuo pronuntiasse: ergo tu filius dei es, ut, quia oblique ostenderat se per scripturas filium dei intellegendum, sic senserint: \'ergo tu dei es filius\', quod te non uis aperte dicere? atque ita et ille (uos dicitis\' confirmatiue respondit, et adeo sic fuit pronuntiatio eius, ut perseuerauerint in eo, quod pronuntiatio sapiebat.
thought_title: Woe to the One Who Betrays the Son of Man
pass_a_gloss: Woe, he says, to him through whom the Son of Man is betrayed. Therefore, now 'woe' is understood to be an exclamation of imprecation and commination, and it is attributed to one who is angry and offended, unless he who was about to relate such a great crime was playing innocently. But if innocently, 'woe' is empty; if not innocently, certainly he is to be punished by him in whom the crime of betrayal was committed. Furthermore, if he knowingly allowed the man, whom he himself had added to his company, to rush into such a great crime, do not now retract concerning the Creator in the case of Adam what can also be retorted against your own god: either he was ignorant, because he did not prevent the one who was about to sin, or he was unable to prevent it, if he was not ignorant, or he did not wish to, if he both knew and was able, and thus he is to be judged malicious, who allowed his man to perish because of a fault. I advise, therefore, that you rather acknowledge the Creator in this case and make him, who is the best God, contrary to your opinion. For even Peter, who spoke something presumptuously, shows a zealous God to you by destining it to denial. He ought to have been betrayed even with a kiss, the prophetic Christ, so that he, the Son, who was loved by the people with their lips, might be known. Having been led into the council, he is asked if he himself is the Christ. Concerning which Christ the Jews would have asked, unless it was about their own? Why, therefore, did he not betray another to them even then? 'So that he might suffer,' you say, that is, so that the best God might plunge the ignorant into crime. But even if he had said it, he would have suffered. For if I say, he says, you will not believe. Furthermore, those who were not going to believe would have persevered in his death. And why would he not have suffered more, if he had manifested himself as the God of another and thus as the adversary of the Creator? Therefore, it was not so that he might suffer that he showed himself to be another at that time, but because they wanted to extort a confession from his mouth, and yet, even if he had confessed, they would not have believed, who ought to have recognized him from his works, which fulfilled the scriptures. Thus, it was his to hide himself, to whom recognition was owed spontaneously. And yet, still stretching out his hand to them: 'From now on,' he says, 'the Son of Man will be sitting at the right hand of the power of God.' For he was suggesting that he was the Son of Man from Daniel's prophecy and the one sitting at the right hand of God from David's psalm. And so, from this statement and the comparison of scripture, they were enlightened, whom he wanted to be understood: 'Therefore, you are the Son of God?' Whose God, if not the one they alone knew? Whose God, if not the one they remembered saying to his Son in the psalm: 'Sit at my right hand?' But he responded: 'You say so,' as if to say: 'Not I.' And yet, he confirmed that he was what they said, while they were asking again. Whence, therefore, will you prove that he spoke interrogatively and not also confirmatively, saying: 'Therefore, you are the Son of God,' so that, because he had shown himself obliquely through the scriptures to be the Son of God, they thus understood: 'Therefore, you are the Son of God,' which you do not want to say openly? And so, he also responded confirmatively, saying 'You say so,' and thus his pronouncement was such that they persevered in what his pronouncement implied.

choices.why: indicating the means by which the Son of Man is betrayed
indicating that God knowingly permitted the crime
indicating that God would be considered malicious if he allowed his man to perish

pass_b_english: "Woe," he says, "to the man through whom the Son of Man is betrayed." So now "woe" stands exposed as an outcry of curse and threat, attributed to one who is angry and offended — unless the betrayer was merely playing the innocent while handing over so monstrous a crime. But if he acted innocently, the "woe" is empty; if not, then the one in whom the crime of betrayal lodged must certainly punish him. Furthermore, if the Lord knowingly allowed the man he himself had chosen for his company to rush into such a crime, do not now backtrack on the Creator's conduct toward Adam — arguments that boomerang against your own god. Either that god was ignorant, since he did not prevent the coming sinner from providence; or he was unable to stop it, if he was not ignorant; or he was unwilling, if he both knew and could — and thus he must be judged malicious for letting his own man perish through a fault. I urge you, therefore, to acknowledge the Creator in this instance rather than make a rival god who is "best" contrary to your own position. For even Peter, by speaking presumptuously, shows you a zealous God by destining that presumption for denial. He ought to have been betrayed even with a kiss — the prophetic Christ — so that he, the Son who was loved by the people with their lips, might be recognized. Led into the council, he is asked whether he himself is the Christ. About which Christ would the Jews have asked, if not their own? Why then did he not betray another to them even then? "So that he might suffer," you say — that is, so that the "best" God might plunge the ignorant into crime. Yet even if he had said it, he would have suffered. "For if I tell you," he says, "you will not believe" (Luke 22:67). And those who were not going to believe would have persisted in his death regardless. And why would he not have suffered all the more, if he had revealed himself as another's God and thereby the Creator's adversary? Therefore, it was not to suffer that he refrained from showing himself as another then, but because they wanted to extort a confession from his mouth — and yet, even had he confessed, they would not have believed, though they ought to have recognized him from his works fulfilling the Scriptures. So it fell to him to hide himself, to whom recognition was owed freely. And still he stretches out his hand to them: "From now on the Son of Man will be seated at the right hand of the power of God" (Luke 22:69). For he was signaling that he is the Son of Man from Daniel's prophecy (Daniel 7:13) and the one seated at God's right hand from David's psalm (Psalm 110:1). Illuminated by this statement and the comparison of Scripture, those he wanted to understand grasped it: "Are you then the Son of God?" Whose God, if not the only one they knew? Whose God, if not the one they remembered saying to his Son in the psalm: "Sit at my right hand"? He answered, "You say so" — as if to say: "Not I." Yet he confirmed that he is exactly what they said, even as they pressed the question again. How then will you prove he spoke interrogatively and not also confirmatively — declaring, "So you are the Son of God" — so that, because he had shown himself obliquely through the Scriptures to be understood as the Son of God, they thus understood: "So you are the Son of God," which you refuse to say openly? And so he too responded confirmatively with "You say so," and his pronouncement was such that they persisted in what his pronouncement implied.
